about: Consolidation, Integration and Feedback Week C (MBBS0022) is a 0-credit Term 3 week in UCL's MBBS Year 1, described in the 2026/27 module catalogue as the third of three core teaching weeks of this kind. It is timetabled for late April or early May, after Fluids, Nutrition and Metabolism, and is designed to help students consolidate and integrate the preceding modules, with feedback. UCL's 2026–27 Year 1 assessment guide describes formative papers only for the November and February CIF weeks, so this guide focuses on integrating the year and planning for the end-of-year Applied Knowledge Tests; it does not invent a syllabus.

notes.h: What CIF Week C is and where it fits
notes.body:
Consolidation, Integration and Feedback Week C (MBBS0022) is not a taught subject with its own syllabus. UCL's 2026/27 module catalogue describes it as the third of three core teaching weeks of this kind in Year 1.

What the official module page says
- It is designed to help you consolidate and integrate the preceding modules, and it includes feedback.
- It is timetabled for late April or early May, in Term 3.
- It is taught in person, carries 0 credits and is open only to students on the MBBS programme.

Where it sits in the year
- Year 1 runs: Introduction and Orientation; Foundations of Health and Medical Practice; Infection and Defence; CIF A (end of November into early December); Circulation and Breathing; CIF B (February); Fluids, Nutrition and Metabolism; then CIF C.
- In UCL's 2026–27 overall timetable, CIF C comes at the end of Fluids, Nutrition and Metabolism, after the Easter break, in late April to early May 2027 (weeks beginning 26 April and 3 May 2027). Check the current Year 1 timetable on Moodle for exact dates.
- The Clinical and Professional Practice strands (such as Anatomy and Imaging, and Use of Medicines) run alongside the systems modules all year, so they are part of what you are consolidating too.
- After CIF C, the next big milestone is the pair of summative Applied Knowledge Test papers at the end of the year.

How CIF C differs from A and B
- UCL's 2026–27 Year 1 Format of Assessments document describes online formative papers in the November and February CIF weeks (the February one as a mock under exam conditions). It does not describe a formative paper for CIF C.
- So do not assume there is a third mock. The catalogue says the week includes feedback; check Moodle for what form that takes in your year.

Background from an older guide
- UCL's Year 1 Study Guide from 2018–19 said each CIF week followed one of the horizontal modules (CIF C followed Fluids, Nutrition and Metabolism) and was meant to revise the preceding module, integrate it with the other modules and strands, and give feedback.
- That guide described assessments in force at the time, which differ from the current integrated online format. Treat it as background only.

Why it matters
- CIF C is the last structured review week before the summative AKTs. Fluids, Nutrition and Metabolism is the most recent module and the one you have had least time to revise, so the week is a chance to secure it and link it to everything earlier.

Exam tips: use CIF C to close gaps, not to start revision from scratch. Arrive with a list of topics you know are weak.

notes.h: Integrating material from the year's modules
notes.body:
'Integration' appears in the name of the week because UCL's summative assessments integrate across modules and disciplines. The 2026–27 Year 1 Format of Assessments says the papers are blueprinted to the year of study, the UCL Curriculum Map and the GMC's Good medical practice and Outcomes for graduates, and test intellectual and practical skills rather than simple recall. This note shows how to revise in a joined-up way; it is not a syllabus.

Why integrate?
- Real patients do not arrive sorted by module. A single SBA stem can test anatomy, physiology, pathology, pharmacology principles and communication at once.
- Linking topics makes them easier to remember, because each fact sits in a network rather than alone.

Themes that cross Year 1 modules (examples using standard science)
- Oxygen from air to mitochondria: ventilation and gas exchange (Circulation and Breathing) deliver oxygen; cardiac output and haemoglobin carry it; in cells it is the final electron acceptor in oxidative phosphorylation, which produces most ATP from glucose and fat (metabolism).
- Fluid balance and blood pressure: water is distributed between intracellular and extracellular compartments; plasma volume affects venous return, cardiac output and blood pressure; the kidney, renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system and ADH adjust volume over hours to days.
- Infection meets organ systems: pneumonia combines microbiology and immune responses (Infection and Defence) with impaired gas exchange and oxygen therapy (Circulation and Breathing); sepsis links infection with failing circulation.
- Evidence and data: the statistics and epidemiology from Foundations apply to every system, for example interpreting a reference range for blood glucose or judging the evidence for a cardiovascular drug.
- People and society: risk factors such as smoking, diet and deprivation link the sociology from Foundations to heart and lung disease and to nutrition-related disease.

Practical ways to integrate
- Concept maps: put a core idea (for example 'oxygen delivery' or 'energy balance') in the centre and branch out to each module and strand.
- Case-based revision: take a common presentation (breathlessness, weight loss, fever) and work through the anatomy, physiology, pathology, investigations and principles of treatment.
- Question banks with mixed topics: random mixed blocks are harder than single-topic practice but closer to the real papers.
- Teach each other: explaining links aloud to a study partner shows you where your understanding is thin.

Exam tips: for every topic you revise, write one 'link' sentence connecting it to a different module; these links are what integrated questions test.

notes.h: Using feedback and planning for the end-of-year AKTs
notes.body:
CIF C comes shortly before the summative assessments, so the feedback you have built up across the year should now drive a final revision plan.

What the summative assessment looks like (2026–27)
- UCL's 2026–27 Year 1 Format of Assessments describes two Applied Knowledge Test papers.
- Each is a two-hour online integrated paper worth no more than 100 marks.
- Questions are a mix of Single Best Answer (SBA) and Very Short Answer (VSA) items, and may include images. The document gives the five-option SBA and five-word VSA limits in its description of the formatives, which are designed to let you experience all the summative question types.
- There is no negative marking, so always answer every question.
- Pacing: 120 minutes for up to 100 marks is about 1.2 minutes per mark.
- UCL directs students to sample questions on the Assessment Unit Moodle site, and to read UCL's Examination Guide for Candidates, the Medical School's assessment policies and the MBBS mark scheme before the exams.

Pulling your feedback together
- Gather your results and notes from the CIF A and CIF B formative papers and any in-module quizzes.
- List recurring weak areas by module, by discipline (for example anatomy, biochemistry, pharmacology principles, statistics) and by question type.
- Rank them by how weak you are and how much of the year they cover. Fix big, weak areas first.

Building a plan for the final weeks
- Use the Moodle learning objectives for each module as the master checklist.
- Mix topics in each session (interleaving) and revisit each one several times with gaps between (spaced repetition).
- Make retrieval the main activity: timed SBA blocks, VSA-style recall (write a short answer before looking at any options), flashcards, and drawing key diagrams from memory.
- Keep a running 'error log': each wrong answer, why you got it wrong, and the correct principle.
- Schedule at least one full timed practice paper so you test your pacing over two hours.

Looking after yourself
- Plan rest days and sleep. Tired revision is inefficient.
- If something is affecting your studies, talk to your personal tutor early. UCL Medical School has a student support team, and UCL's wider well-being services are available. If illness or other circumstances affect an assessment, find out about UCL's extenuating circumstances process in good time.

Exam tips: in the final week, stop learning new detail and focus on practice questions and your error log.

notes.h: Practice questions in the SBA and VSA styles
notes.body:
The questions in this section practise UCL's formats (five-option SBA, and short recall answers like VSAs) using standard basic science about body fluids and metabolism. They are not taken from UCL papers, and UCL does not publish a CIF C question paper or a detailed Fluids, Nutrition and Metabolism topic list in its catalogue, so check coverage against the Moodle learning objectives.

How to use them
- Cover the options, answer first, then compare. For VSA-style items, write no more than five words.
- Read every explanation: each distractor is based on a common confusion.

Core ideas these questions draw on (approximate textbook values)
- Body water: in an adult man, total body water is roughly 60% of body weight. About two-thirds is intracellular and one-third extracellular; plasma is about a quarter of the extracellular fluid and interstitial fluid about three-quarters.
- Worked example for a 70 kg man: total body water about 42 L; intracellular about 28 L; extracellular about 14 L; plasma about 3.5 L; interstitial fluid about 10.5 L.
- Ions: sodium is the main extracellular cation and potassium the main intracellular cation, maintained by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase.
- Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. It acts on V2 receptors in the collecting duct, inserting aquaporin-2 water channels so more water is reabsorbed. Aldosterone, by contrast, increases sodium reabsorption in the distal nephron.
- The pancreatic islets: β-cells secrete insulin, α-cells secrete glucagon and δ-cells secrete somatostatin. The exocrine acinar cells secrete digestive enzymes.
- Glycolysis takes place in the cytoplasm and gives a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose, producing pyruvate.

Exam tips: build your own short bank from your Fluids, Nutrition and Metabolism objectives: one SBA and one VSA for each objective, then swap with a friend.

questions.q: A healthy 70 kg man has total body water of about 60% of body weight. Approximately what is his plasma volume?
questions.why: Total body water ≈ 0.6 × 70 = 42 L; extracellular fluid is about one-third (14 L) and plasma about a quarter of that, ≈ 3.5 L. 42 L is total body water. 28 L is the intracellular fluid (two-thirds of total body water). 14 L is the whole extracellular fluid, of which plasma is only part. 10.5 L is the interstitial fluid, the other three-quarters of the extracellular fluid.

questions.q: How does antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) reduce urine volume?
options: By constricting the efferent arteriole to raise filtration
By increasing glomerular filtration rate through afferent arteriole dilation
By stimulating sodium reabsorption through epithelial sodium channels in the distal nephron
By inserting aquaporin-2 water channels into collecting duct cells
By inhibiting the Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ co-transporter in the loop of Henle
questions.why: ADH acts on V2 receptors in collecting duct cells, which insert aquaporin-2 channels so more water is reabsorbed and urine becomes concentrated. Stimulating sodium reabsorption through epithelial sodium channels is the main action of aldosterone, a common mix-up. Inhibiting the Na⁺/K⁺/2Cl⁻ co-transporter is how loop diuretics work, and it increases urine volume. Efferent arteriolar constriction is an action of angiotensin II. Increasing filtration would tend to increase, not reduce, urine output.

questions.q: Which cells of the pancreas secrete insulin?
questions.why: Insulin is secreted by the β-cells of the islets of Langerhans. α-cells secrete glucagon, insulin's main counter-regulatory hormone, so they are easy to confuse. Acinar cells form the exocrine pancreas and secrete digestive enzymes. δ-cells secrete somatostatin. Hepatocytes are liver cells, a major target of insulin rather than its source.

questions.q: Describe four evidence-based strategies for using the weeks around CIF C to prepare for the end-of-year Applied Knowledge Tests.
markScheme: Use feedback from CIF A and B formatives to identify and rank weak areas (by module, discipline, question type)
Retrieval practice: timed mixed SBA blocks and VSA-style recall rather than rereading
Spaced repetition and interleaving of topics across modules, using Moodle learning objectives as a checklist
Full timed practice paper to rehearse pacing (about 1.2 minutes per mark) and answer every question as there is no negative marking; keep an error log; look after well-being
questions.modelAnswer: First, gather the feedback from the CIF A and CIF B formative papers and rank weak areas by module, discipline and question type, so revision targets the biggest gaps. Second, make retrieval practice the core activity: timed mixed SBA blocks and VSA-style recall, writing an answer before looking at any options, rather than rereading notes. Third, space and interleave revision, returning to each topic several times and mixing topics from different modules, using the Moodle learning objectives as the checklist. Fourth, sit at least one full timed practice paper to rehearse pacing; two hours for up to 100 marks is about 1.2 minutes per mark, and because there is no negative marking every question should be answered. Keeping an error log and protecting sleep and rest make these strategies more effective.

questions.q: VSA practice (no more than five words each): (a) Name the main intracellular cation. (b) State the net number of ATP molecules gained from glycolysis of one glucose molecule.
